title: NYU Curriculum Alignment
subtitle: A curriculum redesign that connected Information Architecture education to modern UX practice, research, and evidence-based decision-making.

sections.heading: The Conflict
body: At NYU, students were learning Information Architecture at a moment when the UX field was rapidly changing. Traditional IA methods still mattered, but students were at risk of learning structure without enough exposure to user behavior, research, testing, and evidence-based decision-making.
They could create site maps and navigation systems, but many had not yet learned how to validate whether those structures made sense to real people.

image.caption: The course needed to reflect where the UX field was going, not only where IA had been.

sections.heading: The Strategic Action
body: Van recognized that the curriculum needed to meet the reality of the industry. He expanded the course beyond static organization and classification methods, introducing students to the broader discipline of user experience design.

He reframed Information Architecture as part of a larger human-centered process. Students learned to consider user goals, behavioral patterns, research findings, usability principles, and real-world context.
The classroom became a bridge between academic design training and professional UX practice.
bullets: Expanded the course beyond static organization and classification methods.
Connected IA to user goals, behavior, research, usability, and real-world context.
Helped students practice evidence-based design decision-making.

sections.heading: Impact Beyond the Classroom
body: The curriculum helped students understand that good design begins with evidence, not personal preference or internal logic.
It created a UX-centered learning experience for 60+ students annually, influencing the career development of roughly 300 designers over time.
bullets: Student win: Helped students understand that good design begins with evidence.
Professional win: Created a UX-centered learning experience for 60+ students annually, influencing roughly 300 designers over time.
Industry win: Prepared students for modern design teams where research, testing, iteration, and cross-functional collaboration are core skills.
Strategic win: Shifted the educational focus from structured site maps to evidence-based design decisions.
Teaching win: Treated curriculum design as a service design problem centered on student capability.

image.caption: Curriculum design became a way to prepare emerging designers for modern practice.

sections.heading: Strategic Takeaway
body: Van helped students move from organizing information to understanding people.

The larger contribution was not simply teaching a class. It was updating the learning model so emerging designers could enter the field with a stronger foundation in research, empathy, and evidence-based practice.
